title: Four friends for four seasons
hookLine: riddles about fish and rivers, then four friends for four seasons, and the last friend is what you gave
carry: dana: what you give goes with you

lines: WHAT SLEEPS WITH ITS EYES OPEN?
A FISH, AN EGG, A STONE, A RIVER.
cards: What sleeps with its eyes open? The yaksha keeps going, and some of the questions are pure fun. A fish, Yudhishthira answers.
What doesn't move once it's born? An egg. What has no heart?
A stone. What grows by its own force? A river.
Four brothers lie dead on the shore, and the talk sounds almost like a game by a campfire. Then the questions turn toward people.

teach.b: Who is the friend of a traveler far from home? A companion on the road, Yudhishthira answers. The friend of someone who keeps a home?
Of someone who is sick? The physician. And of someone about to die?
Charity, the gifts they've given. Four friends for four seasons of a life. Remember who is answering: a man in exile, whose companions on the road lie dead behind him.
Hold on to that last friend, because it's a big Hindu teaching. Hindus call it dana, giving.

teach.h: DANA: WHAT YOU GIVE GOES WITH YOU.
teach.b: Wealth stays behind when you die; what you gave goes with you, as your karma.
It's why giving runs through Hindu life: food at the temple, money in the hundi, gifts at a birth or a wedding, and in the name of loved ones who have died. Then the yaksha asks about letting go.
What, given up, makes you agreeable? Pride. What leaves no regret?
Anger. What makes you rich, once you let it go? Desire.
And what makes you happy, once it's gone? Greed. Hindu teachers count six inner enemies: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy.
Four of them are right here at the lake. Notice they fit together. Greed holds on; dana lets go.
The answers come out plain and small, from a man whose brothers' lives depend on them.

how: The middle of the Yaksha's questions mixes riddles about fish and rivers with plain guidance: the friend of the dying is charity, dana, and pride, anger, desire and greed are worth giving up.

o: a friend, someone who stands by you
a guest who must be fed before the host
a teacher who guides a student's studies

games.q: the friends of every season — tap the pairs.

s: Yudhishthira said the friend of the dying is the gods
he said charity: the gifts a person has given.
giving up desire, he said, makes a person rich
and giving up greed makes a person happy.
in Hindu teaching, the wealth you save goes with you when you die
what goes with you is what you gave: dana, the friend of the dying.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. the yaksha asks: what, if you give it up, leaves no regret? what do you answer?
games.why: anger. and alongside it: give up pride and you're agreeable, desire and you're rich, greed and you're happy.

practice: Bring to mind, one at a time, the friends of your own seasons: someone who was a companion when you were far from home, someone who shares your home, someone who looked after you when you were sick.
Let each face stay for a few breaths, and thank them silently. Then choose one small gift to give today, food, time or money, given quietly. If you pray, you can offer it in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Mitra, a friend, is what the yaksha asks about: for a traveler, a householder, the sick and the dying. Four friends for four seasons, and the last one is dana, what you gave. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: mitra, a friend; the yaksha asks who is the friend of each kind of person.

carryVoice: Your line: dana, what you give goes with you. Four friends for four seasons, and the last one is what you gave away. That's day eight hundred four.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the episode of the Yaksha's questions: the riddles (fish, egg, stone, river); the friend of the exile, householder, sick and dying; what is renounced (pride, anger, desire, greed)
Dana (giving) in Hindu practice, and the six inner enemies (kama, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, matsarya), in general
